Table 4-10  Conditions of Pediatric Patients at Risk for Refeeding Syndrome
•	 Protein-calorie malnutrition (e.g., refugees or famine victims)
•	 Chronic conditions causing malnutrition (uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, cancer, congenital heart disease, 
chronic liver disease, and neglect)
•	 Malabsorptive sydromes (including inflammatory bowel disease, cystic fibrosis, chronic pancreatitis, and short 
bowel syndrome)
•	 Morbid obesity with massive weight loss of 10% within the past 2 months
•	 IV hydration without provision of sufficient calories and protein for 10–14 days
•	 Anorexia nervosa
•	 Patients <80% of ideal body weight (defined as 50% weight for stature)
•	 Dysphagia caused by neuromuscular diseases (e.g., cerebral palsy)
Source:  John A. Kerner and Jo Ann T. Hattner. 2014. Used with permission.


Case 2  Malnutrition and Refeeding Syndrome in Children 
185
Sodium Retention Sodium retention is also seen in refeeding syndrome. The infusion of carbo­
hydrates leads to increased insulin secretion. Insulin causes decreased renal excretion of sodium 
and water. Patients may then develop fluid overload, pulmonary edema, and congestive cardiac 
failure. Low serum albumin may also contribute to edema during refeeding as a result of low 
oncotic pressure.
Thiamin Vitamin deficiencies also occur because of inadequate intake. Deficiency in thiamin 
(vitamin B1) has important consequences during refeeding. It is an important cofactor for enzymes 
needed in carbohydrate metabolism, and it is rapidly consumed in glycolysis during refeeding
